newsitem.title: UK: Seventh Briton dies from E coli, inquiry ordered.
newsitem.headline: Seventh Briton dies from E coli, inquiry ordered.

text.p: A seventh person died on Wednesday from an outbreak of food poisoning in Scotland caused by the E coli bacteria and the government set up an inquiry in the face of accusations it had not acted quickly enough to save lives.
Health authorities in Lanarkshire county, where the outbreak occurred, said the victim was a 74-year-old man.

All the victims have been elderly, but more than 260 people of all ages have reported symptoms and several children are in hospital after being hit by the bacteria, which can cause brain damage and kidney failure.
Britain's Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth, denying tardiness by any government department, pointed a finger of suspicion at a butcher at the centre of the outbreak.

"The thing that is causing me most anxiety are the reports we are getting from the local authority that the meat was supplied ... by the butcher the day after he agreed to cease the sale of cooked meat," Forsyth said on BBC radio.
Strathclyde Police are investigating allegations that the prize-winning butcher linked to the outbreak supplied cooked meat to a birthday party after being ordered to stop selling it.
The butcher's firm said through its lawyer that it had cooperated fully with the authorities.
E coli is a common gut bacteria that is normally harmless, but a toxic strain that lives in cattle can be passed to humans via manure or improper slaughtering.

The Scottish office has said local health authorities, not the government, had taken the decision not to name, for five days after the outbreak began, outlets that had bought meat from the butcher involved.
The popular Scottish Daily Record newspaper said "the normally sure-footed Forsyth is stumbling and bumbling".
"The public urgently need answers to vital questions. Yet all they hear is the sound of the buck being passed," it added.

The parents of seven children who suffered food poisoning from E coli in England this summer said they had been granted legal aid to sue the Department of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food.
The families allege the government departments failed to inform the public of the dangers of the E coli bacteria and did not ensure food manufacturers warned of it on labelling.
